title: The Decoy Effect
description: Adding a clearly inferior third option makes one of the original two look much better. It’s a phantom option designed to push you.
shortDescription: Adding a clearly inferior third option makes one of the original two look much better. It’s a phantom option designed to push you.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: Adding a clearly inferior third option makes one of the original two look much better. It’s a phantom option designed to push you.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A cinema offers a small popcorn for $4, a medium for $7.50, and a large for $8. The medium seems like a rip‑off; most people buy the large because “it’s only 50 cents more.” The medium was never meant to sell.
A software subscription: Basic at $10, Pro at $25, and Premium at $30. Pro looks bad compared to Premium, so people jump to the expensive one.
A car dealer shows you a base model at $20k, a mid‑trim at $27k, and the high‑trim at $28k. You skip the base and mid, feeling smart for “only” paying $1k more for the top. The mid‑trim is the decoy.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Always choosing the option that seems like a “bargain” compared to a worse‑value alternative.
Feeling you got a great deal, though you spent more than intended.
Choosing an option you wouldn’t have selected if the decoy weren’t there.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “For just a little more, I might as well get the best one.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: One option seems clearly overpriced compared to its neighbors.
You’re comparing options relative to each other rather than to your actual needs.
You go in planning to spend less and end up spending more without much resistance.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: We make relative judgments, not absolute ones. The decoy provides a frame of reference that makes the target option (usually the most expensive) appear disproportionately valuable. This exploits the contrast principle.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Before choosing, ask: “If that middle option didn’t exist, what would I pick?”
Decide your budget and must‑have features before seeing the pricing table.
Treat each option as if it’s the only one available, and ask whether it’s worth the price.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Thinking you’re immune because you “spotted” the decoy. You may still shift your preference, just less.
Assuming decoys are always obvious. Subtle decoys work best.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: An online magazine offers a digital subscription for $59 and a digital‑plus‑print combo for $60. You pick the combo because it seems a steal. The digital‑only was the decoy. Most readers never use the print, but they paid an extra dollar that, at scale, rakes in millions.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: If one option looks absurdly bad, it’s probably there on purpose—to make another option look absurdly good. Judge each on its own merit.
